question: How does Nir Eyal explain why people procrastinate, and what does he recommend doing when discomfort makes them want to get distracted?

S1.title: Strategies for becoming less distractible and improving focus | Nir Eyal
S1.text:

If you're constantly thinking, "Ugh, that project is going to suck. I don't really want to work on it. I don't want to make those sales calls. I don't want to make that presentation. I don't want to do that thing that feels uncomfortable," and you don't have the tools to deal with that discomfort, you're always going to procrastinate because fundamentally, procrastination is an emotion regulation problem. It's not a character flaw. There's nothing wrong with you, you're not broken. It's just that you don't have the tools to deal with emotional discomfort and that's the part that everybody skips over. So, we don't want to talk about these uncomfortable feelings, but that's where it has to start. And then, the part that people don't do is actually planning out not the task itself, but the time to work on the task without distraction. That's the part that if you can implement that step two that I talked about of making time for traction, that becomes a game changer.

So, what I do is I take a deep breath and I repeat a mantra that I made up for myself. You can make up your own mantra. My personal mantra whenever I feel this internal trigger is I remind myself this. I say, "This is what it feels like to get better. This is what it feels like to get better." And just saying that for as long as I need to until that emotion crests and subsides and then get back to work. What you'll find nine times out of 10 is that by the time those 10 minutes are up, you will have forgotten about that sensation. You'll be right back at the task at hand. And so, that's what's called the 10-minute rule. And of course what you're doing over time is that the 10-minute rule can become the 12-minute rule, can become the 20-minute rule, and most importantly, you are proving to yourself that you have agency that you said you were going to focus on a task and you did. That's the most important part.

It's not being stolen, we're giving it away. And so, what we need to do is to empower ourselves by showing ourselves in practice as well as in theory that we can postpone that distraction when we say we will.

What I found in my research writing this book is that high performers in every industry, business, the arts, sports, high performers, they feel the same internal triggers. They also feel lonely. They also feel bored. They also feel stressed. They also feel anxious, but they use that discomfort like a rocket fuel to propel them towards traction. Whereas what distractable people do, as soon as they feel uncomfortable, as soon as they feel bored, as soon as they feel lonesome, as soon as soon as they feel indecisive or stressed, boom, they're escaping it with a drink, with a click, with something to take their mind off of that discomfort. So, that has to be step number one.

answer.summary: Nir Eyal says procrastination is an emotion-regulation problem, not a character flaw: people avoid tasks to escape discomfort. He recommends noticing the internal trigger, letting the feeling pass with tools such as the 10-minute rule, then returning to the task.

sections.heading: Why people procrastinate
sections.content: Eyal explains that when a task feels uncomfortable—because it seems difficult, boring, frustrating, or anxiety-provoking—people may procrastinate to avoid those feelings. He calls procrastination an emotion-regulation problem, not a character flaw or evidence that someone is broken. In his account, many distractions come from internal triggers rather than technology itself.

sections.heading: What to do when discomfort prompts distraction
sections.content: First identify the internal trigger—the feeling or “itch” you are trying to escape—and recognize it as a feeling. Eyal’s example is to take a deep breath, acknowledge that the work is hard and that frustration or anxiety is understandable, then repeat a personal mantra: “This is what it feels like to get better.” Use the 10-minute rule: wait with the feeling until it crests and subsides, then return to the task. He says the interval can grow over time (for example, to 12 or 20 minutes), helping you practice postponing distraction and build confidence that you can follow through.

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately explains procrastination as an attempt to regulate emotions and escape discomfort, and recommends noticing the trigger and using the 10-minute rule. It does not mention putting the intended work on the calendar, a required reference point.

previous_judgments.explanation: The answer accurately explains that procrastination is driven by avoiding emotional discomfort and gives supported advice to notice the trigger and use the 10-minute rule. However, it omits Eyal’s recommendation to schedule the intended work on the calendar, so it does not cover all expected points.
